# Global conic rigidity for tetrahedral sections with two noncentral coordinates

Let Xi be uniform on the probability tetrahedron. Let b=(a,c,b_3,b_4) be an interior barycentric point with a,c>1/3. Three distinct strict quadrilateral section planes, each having actual section centroid b, cannot have linearly dependent raw normals unless b_3=b_4.

The statement is global. It includes a=c, accounts for the resulting degenerate conic, and requires no continuation from a symmetric example. As a consequence, a tetrahedral positive-weight capacity global maximizer chosen with the fewest active rows cannot have exactly three full rows and two noncentral common section-centroid coordinates. Indeed its three distinct raw normals sum to zero; the present theorem forces an equal central pair, and `candidate 03420419c4771251` supplies a strict feasible improvement in that case. This is an ordinary stochastic-capacity structural theorem, not a proof of OC.

## 1. Coordinates and one universal conic identity

Use

    A=3a-1>0, B=3c-1>0,
    G=1-3b_3, D=1-3b_4,
    U=A+B, V=AB, W=GD.

Then G+D=1+U, 0<G,D<1, 0<U<1, and G,D>U. Consequently

    W>U>V,                                         (1)

where W>U follows from (G-U)(D-U)=W-U>0, and V<=U^2/4<U.

The same-side noncentral theorem makes the unoriented split of every admitted plane {1,2}|{3,4}. Orient it toward the first pair and normalize its fourth raw entry to -1. Its normal is

    C=(p,q,-r,-1), p,q,r>0,
    q=[G-U+(1-G)r-(1+A)p]/(1+B).                   (2)

The second equation is exactly C dot b=0. Define the following six polynomials in A,B,G, with D=1+A+B-G:

    c0=(G-A)^2(G-A-B),
    c3=(A-B)(1+A)(G-D),
    c5=(G-1)(G-1-B)^2,

    c1=-2A^3-A^2B+5A^2G-2A^2+AB^2
          -3AG^2+3AG-B^2G+BG^2+BG-2G^2,
    c4=-c1(A,B,D),
    c2=-(G-D)(AB+2A-GD).

Here c1(A,B,D) means substitution of D for the third argument of the displayed polynomial. Every actual section with centroid b satisfies

    C_b(p,r):=c0+c1 p+c2 r+c3 p^2+c4 pr+c5 r^2=0.  (3)

Equation (3) is an algebraic identity of the actual centroid map. It does not assume a finite inverse map, discard roots, or divide by A-B or G-D. For a direct verification put X=1/p,Y=1/q,Z=1/r,W0=1, L=X+Y+Z+W0. The actual section centroid is

    3a=X/(X+Z)+X/(X+W0)-X/L,
    3c=Y/(Y+Z)+Y/(Y+W0)-Y/L,
    3b_3=Z/(Z+X)+Z/(Z+Y)-Z/L,
    3b_4=W0/(W0+X)+W0/(W0+Y)-W0/L.                (4)

These formulas follow by triangulating the quadrilateral on its diagonals. Substitute A=3a-1, B=3c-1, G=1-3b_3 from (4) into the left side of (3). Clearing its positive denominators and expanding gives zero identically in p,q,r. Thus (3) applies to every positive strict-quadrilateral parameter, including all equal-height cases. The accompanying exact verifier performs this direct identity check; the full six coefficients above make the identity independently reproducible.

The symmetric matrix of the homogeneous conic in coordinates (p,r,1) has determinant

    det [[c3,c4/2,c1/2],
         [c4/2,c5,c2/2],
         [c1/2,c2/2,c0]]
       =(A-B)(1+B)(G-D)(AB-GD)^2/4.                (5)

This is a second exact polynomial identity.

## 2. Both pairs unequal: no three collinear normals

If A!=B and G!=D, (1) and (5) make the conic nondegenerate. A nondegenerate projective conic contains no three distinct collinear points. For completeness, restricting its homogeneous quadratic to a line gives a polynomial of degree at most two. Three distinct zeros would make the restriction identically zero, so the line would divide the quadratic. A quadratic with a line factor has singular matrix, contradicting (5).

Linear dependence of three distinct normalized normals C_i in (2) would give coefficients t_i, not all zero, with sum t_i=0 (fourth coordinate) and sum t_i(p_i,r_i)=0. Therefore their three distinct points (p_i,r_i) would be collinear. Distinctness follows because (2) recovers q uniquely from p,r. This is impossible by the preceding paragraph.

It remains to handle A=B and G!=D. This case cannot be removed by perturbation or by dividing (5) by A-B.

## 3. The degenerate conic when the noncentral pair agrees

Set B=A. Direct factorization of (3) gives exactly

    C_b(p,r)
       =[2(1+A)p+(G-1)r+2A-G]
        *[(1+A-G)^2 r-(A-G)^2].                    (6)

The first line L1 is precisely p=q. The second line L2 is horizontal:

    r=R^2, R=(G-A)/(1+A-G)>0.                      (7)

Both numerator and denominator in R are positive because 2A<G<1. Moreover R!=1 because G!=D=1+2A-G. The two lines are distinct.

We prove that L1 contains at most one actual common-centroid section and L2 at most two. It will then follow that no line contains three such sections: any other line intersects the union L1 union L2 in at most two points.

## 4. At most one actual section on p=q

On L1 the through-b relation is

    p=q=[G-2A+(1-G)r]/[2(1+A)], r>0.               (8)

Since 2A<G<1, this is a connected positive strict-quadrilateral family for every r>0. Let P(r)=Pr(C(r) dot Xi>=0) be its actual cap fraction. It is smooth.

A stationary point P'(r)=0 is equivalent to the section centroid being b. To see this, every section in this family has equal first two centroid coordinates. Its centroid lies in C(r)^perp. At a stationary point it also lies in C'(r)^perp, by the ordinary cap first variation. The independent vectors C(r),C'(r) span the two-dimensional space of through-b normals whose first two entries agree. Its orthogonal complement is span{b,e_1-e_2}. Equality of the first two centroid coordinates, followed by the sum-one normalization, therefore forces the actual centroid to be b. The converse is the same first-variation identity.

At every such critical point, P''(r)>0. Indeed orient the complementary cap toward its two central vertices 3,4. The already proved captured-central-pair curvature theorem gives strictly negative complementary cap curvature on v=b_4 e_3-b_3 e_4, so the displayed cap has v^T Hess(P)v>0. The vectors C,v span the same two-dimensional through-b normal space. The nonradial direction C' is therefore mu C+nu v with nu!=0. Degree-zero homogeneity gives Hess(P)C=-grad(P); at a stationary centroid grad(P) is proportional to b, so all radial and radial-cross terms vanish on this space. Hence

    P''(r)=nu^2 v^T Hess(P)v>0.

A smooth real function on an interval cannot have two critical points if every critical point has strictly positive second derivative. If two existed, choose a point just to the right of the first where P'>0 and a point just to the left of the second where P'<0. The function attains an interior maximum between them, giving a critical point with P''<=0, a contradiction. Thus L1 contains at most one actual section.

The only nonstandard curvature input in this step is the fully proved central-pair cap lemma in `candidate 8704554a92158bfc`, in the local form used and independently audited in `candidate a5d3d44181ebed82`. No assertion about the Hessian of an arbitrary noncentral pair is used.

## 5. At most two actual sections on the horizontal line

On L2 put r=R^2 and

    s=p+q=[G-2A+(1-G)R^2]/(1+A)>0.

Using G=A+R/(1+R), equivalently

    s=[R-A(R^2+1)]/(1+A)>0.                        (9)

Consider first p!=q. In unnormalized reciprocal diagonal coordinates X=1/p,Y=1/q,Z=1/r,W0=1, put M=XY=1/(pq), N=ZW0=1/r, T=X+Y+Z+W0. Equality of the first two actual centroid coordinates gives

    N T^2=(M-N)^2.                                 (10)

Also M>N. To verify the sign, normalize the four diagonal coordinates to sum one and write K=xy-zw. The centroid formula gives

    3a-1=(Kx-zw)/(x-K).

The denominator is (x+z)(x+w)>0 and a>1/3, so K>0. Rescaling back proves M>N.

Writing v=pq, (10) becomes

    [r s+v(r+1)]^2=r(r-v)^2.

All quantities on the left before squaring are positive, and M>N means v<r. Taking the positive square root therefore gives the UNIQUE possible product

    v=v0:=R^2(R-s)/(R^2+R+1).                      (11)

For fixed s this yields at most two asymmetric values of p, exchanged by p and q.

It remains to check that a separate symmetric point p=q=s/2 cannot make a third actual section on L2. At that point put v=s^2/4. Its third centroid coordinate satisfies

    3b_3(actual)=(R^2 s+2v)/(R^4+R^2 s+v)
                       -v/[R^2 s+v(R^2+1)].       (12)

After substituting (9), the following exact identity holds:

    3b_3(actual)-(1-G)=C(A,R)(s^2/4-v0),            (13)

where

    C(A,R)=4(1+A)^2(R-1)[A(R+1)^2+R]
       /[(R+1)(AR^2-A+2R^2+R)
          *(A(R^2-1)^2-R^3-4R^2-R)].

Every factor needed to conclude C!=0 is controlled. R>0, R!=1, A>0. The first nontrivial denominator is (1+A)(2R^2+s)>0. By (9), A<R/(R^2+1), so the last denominator is strictly less than

    -4R^2(R^2+R+1)/(R^2+1)<0.

Thus if the symmetric point has the required centroid, (13) forces v0=s^2/4. The quadratic with sum s and product v0 then has a double root, so the putative two asymmetric sections have coalesced with that symmetric point. Hence L2 contains at most two actual sections in every case, including absence or collision of the asymmetric roots.

Together Sections 3–5 exclude three collinear actual normals when A=B but G!=D.

## 6. Consequence for three full rows

Combining Sections 2 and 3–5 proves the announced global geometric theorem: three distinct actual common-centroid quadrilateral planes with two noncentral centroid coordinates can have linearly dependent normals only when their two central centroid coordinates agree.

At a positive-weight tetrahedral capacity maximum chosen with the fewest active rows, suppose exactly three rows are full and the fourth is zero. The positive-row regularity theorem makes their minimizing cuts proper. If the common section centroid has two coordinates above 1/3, the same-side theorem forces every cut to be a strict quadrilateral of the split used above. Independence of the three active rows implies that their three unoriented normal directions are distinct: if two were proportional, the raw-margin balance would make all three proportional and all rows would lie in span{1,C}, contradicting rank three. Their actual raw margins sum to zero, so they are linearly dependent.

The present theorem therefore forces the equal central pair. The exact three-root reciprocal-stiffness theorem then gives a strictly positive feasible second variation, contradicting maximality. Thus the entire two-noncentral three-full-row stratum is excluded. The unique-noncentral case, in particular different incidence splits around that vertex, is not addressed by this conclusion.

## 7. Unique noncentral coordinate, provided the split is common

The same conic identity gives a further global exclusion with a different hypothesis. Suppose a>1/3 and c,b_3,b_4<=1/3, and three distinct actual common-centroid strict quadrilateral planes ALL have the split {1,2}|{3,4}. Then their normals are linearly independent.

Here A>0, -1<B<=0. The excluded centroid coordinates are strictly less than 1/3: in normalized positive diagonal coordinates, a>1/3 gives K=xy-zw>0, and

    3b_3-1=(-Kz-xy)/(z+K)<0,
    3b_4-1=(-Kw-xy)/(w+K)<0.

Thus G,D>0, while V=AB<=0<W=GD. If G!=D, the determinant (5) is nonzero since A-B>0 and 1+B=3c>0. Section 2 therefore excludes three dependent normals.

If G=D, equality and centrality of b_3,b_4 force equal negative raw heights, by the diagonal-centroid lemma used in the root-interpolation source. Write each representative as (p,q,-1,-1) and define U0=1/(1+p), V0=1/(1+q), T=2-U0-V0. Its actual centroid formulas are

    3a=U0(1+T-U0)/T, 3c=V0(1+T-V0)/T.

The inequalities a>1/3 and c<=1/3 imply U0>T and V0<=T, respectively. Since 0<U0,V0<1, this forces 1/2<T<1. Write B0=b_3=b_4. Every actual section satisfies

    (4B0-T)(2T-1)^2=3(a-c)^2 T.                    (14)

Distinct actual sections have distinct T: their sum U0+V0=2-T and difference U0-V0=3(a-c)T/(2T-1) determine p,q uniquely. If there were three such sections, they would be the three roots of the cubic (14). Its leading coefficient is -4 and Vieta gives

    T1+T2+T3=1+4B0, T1 T2 T3=B0.

Consequently

    T3=(T1+T2-1)/(4T1T2-1)<1/2,

because the denominator is positive and

    2(T1+T2-1)-(4T1T2-1)=-(2T1-1)(2T2-1)<0.

This contradicts the range of every actual root. Thus in this case there are at most two distinct sections altogether. The equality c=1/3 is retained in the inequalities above.

This closes the unique-noncentral three-full-row configuration only when every plane has the same split. The remaining possible configuration must use different splits around the unique noncentral vertex; neither this conic argument nor the root-count step asserts its exclusion.

## 8. A strict sign when an actual section changes split

The same explicit conic retains a useful exact distinction between split types. This section gives a necessary sign for a hypothetical remaining cross-split triple; it does not exclude that triple by itself.

Take any actual strict section with raw margins (p,-r,q,-1), p,q,r>0, and let its actual centroid be b. Form C_b for the OTHER split {1,2}|{3,4} by the coefficients in Section 1. Its normalized coordinates in that conic chart are (p,-q). Direct substitution in the actual centroid formulas gives

    C_b(p,-q)=-N(p,q,r) H(p,q,r)
       /[(p+r)^2(q+1)(q+r)(pqr+pq+pr+qr)^3]<0,      (15)

where

    N=2p^2q^2r+p^2q^2+p^2qr^2+2p^2qr+p^2r^2
        +pq^2r^2+2pq^2r+pqr^2+q^2r^2,

    H=p^4q^4r^2+2p^4q^4r+p^4q^4
      +4p^4q^3r^2+2p^4q^3r+3p^4q^2r^2
      +2p^3q^4r^2+4p^3q^4r+6p^3q^3r^2+4p^3q^2r^2
      +3p^2q^4r^2+4p^2q^3r^3+3p^2q^2r^4
      +6p^2q^2r^3+3p^2q^2r^2+4p^2qr^4+2p^2qr^3+p^2r^4
      +2pq^2r^4+4pq^2r^3+2pqr^4+q^2r^4.

Every coefficient of N,H is positive. Thus the sign is strict in the entire actual strict-quadrilateral domain, with no noncentrality assumption. Equation (15) is a rational identity from the actual section map; the verifier checks it independently of any root parameterization.

Suppose a putative balanced triple has one unique noncentral coordinate and different splits. Orient and normalize its sections toward that vertex. If all cuts are strict quadrilaterals, one normalized point lies strictly between the other two; the middle split must equal an outer split, since a central coordinate negative at both outer points remains negative at their convex combination. Choose the fourth coordinate to be the central vertex excluded by both split types after all normals are oriented toward the noncentral vertex. It is then excluded by every oriented section, so normalization of its raw entry to -1 uses a positive factor in every row and preserves which point lies between the other two. After this specific relabeling, there are two points of one conic and a different-split point outside their interval on the common projective line. The latter has strictly negative conic value by (15). Consequently the quadratic part of the first conic on the chord between its two actual same-split points must be negative. When the conic vanishes identically along that chord this is already impossible.

This is an exact necessary condition retaining the actual split. A general sign theorem for that chord's quadratic part has not been proved here. In particular (15) is not asserted to close the remaining different-split capacity stratum.

For the all-quadrilateral cross-split branch, boundary central coordinates equal to 1/3 are excluded by actual geometry. Every quadrilateral section capturing a noncentral vertex has K=xy-zw>0 in normalized reciprocal diagonal coordinates, and each excluded coordinate satisfies 3b_j-1=(-Kz-xy)/(z+K)<0. The shared split excludes the different split's captured central partner; the different split excludes the shared split's captured central partner; both exclude the remaining central vertex. Hence all three central centroid coordinates are strictly less than 1/3 in any such cross-split triple. This does not discard a triangular or vertex-contact section: those statuses require their separate curvature argument.
